newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Broken U.S. city struggles to shed murder capital tag.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Broken U.S. city struggles to shed murder capital tag.

text.p: A few days ago, eight- year-old Paul Hyde watched someone get shot on television and wondered what it would be like.
So he took the gun hidden under his mother's bed and shot himself through the face. He lived, but why was it so easy for him to get hold of a loaded gun?
If you live in Gary, the reason is obvious.
This grimy steeltown just outside Chicago is not a big place but it is the murder capital of the United States -- awash in a sea of drugs, guns, poverty and despair.
"People are so afraid they sleep on the floor of their apartments in case a bullet comes through the window from a drive-by shooting," said taxi driver Marcelino Galvan.
Washington, Detroit and Los Angeles may be more famous for their mean streets but Gary has more killings per capita than any other city in the U.S.
It first won infamy in 1993 with 110 murders, or more than one for every 1,000 inhabitants. It has stayed top of the polls ever since, chalking up 132 killings last year.
Police, who guard schools to protect children from dealers offering highly-addictive crack cocaine, find themselves battling gangs wearing bulletproof vests and armed with assault rifles.
The drug gangs also fight each other over territory, turning the poorest parts of town into killing zones.
"Sometimes they be shooting and stuff when we at school," said Deona Joiner, aged 12. "It shouldn't be happening."
Founded in 1906, Gary took as its motto "city of the century" and was proud of its key role in the age of heavy industry that lasted until the late 1970s.
The main thoroughfare, Broadway, was once the bustling centre of a prosperous Middle American city where 25,000 people were employed in the steel mills on the shores of Lake Michigan.

Most of the mills have long closed and many people moved away. A few casinos have opened outside the city but the unemployment rate remains stubbornly above 10 percent, almost twice the national rate. Nearly one-third of Gary's 106,000 people live below the poverty line.

There are no hotels and few shops or bars on Broadway, now little more than a semi-derelict thoroughfare that leads out of town. The streets around are dimly lit, the once-proud townhouses gutted or boarded-up.
Many parts of Gary look as if they belong in Bosnia.

There are virtually no campaign posters for the U.S. presidential election. Most of the population is poor and black and there is little question that those who vote will back U.S. President Bill Clinton rather than Republican challenger Bob Dole.
But Clinton's claim to have reduced the crime rate in the United States cuts little ice here, where people have yet to see the results.
Mayor Scott King, elected almost a year ago on promises to clean up the city, has imposed a curfew from 11 p.m. and put more police on the street.
Optimistic that Gary can regain its dignity and prosperity, he is trying to get U.S. government financing to strengthen his overstretched and sometimes outgunned police force of 250 officers.
"We've been much more aggressive in going after the dealers and the gangs," King told Reuters. "The biggest challenge is getting things turned around and people are starting to feel better."
So far this year, there have been nearly 70 murders in Gary but police chief John Roby says many of those have been unrelated to drugs, for the first time in recent years.

"It took 25 years to get in the state we're in and we're not going to turn it around overnight," he said. "My officers have every type of artillery imaginable but the drug dealers can buy the same stuff."
Hazel Newell moved here in 1947 and saw the city in its prime.
"It was beautiful, every store was occupied, the steel mills were going strong," said the 67-year-old pensioner.
"One of the biggest problems is loss of respect in the family. Kids have free run now, the parents are working and there's no one to teach them. It wasn't like that in my day."

Last year, Indiana governor Evan Bayh ordered a force of state troopers into the city for several months in a desperate attempt to stop the blood-letting. The troopers set up roadblocks and the crime rate dropped sharply -- until they were withdrawn several months later.

Whatever measures are taken, the quick profits to be made from drug dealing remain attractive for young people who otherwise face a lifetime of poverty. The stakes are high, with the constant risk of arrest or death at the hands of rival dealers.
Gary has one other claim to fame, as the birthplace of pop superstar Michael Jackson. Perhaps unsurprisingly, the multi- millionaire performer has shown little interest in his hometown.
"He doesn't come to visit," said Galvan. "Not even to perform."
